sections.title: How does the Projectile motion calculator work?
sections.html:
The Projectile motion calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the angle of launch (α), the time of flight (t) and the time.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Projectile motion calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ)=initial velocity (V) × the cosine of (angle of launch (α))
Initial vertical velocity (Vy)=initial velocity (V) × the sine of (angle of launch (α))
Initial vertical velocity (Vy)=-initial height (h) ÷ time of flight (t) + (1 ÷ 2) × time of flight (t) × gravitational acceleration
Distance (d)=horizontal velocity × time of flight (t)
Initial height (h)=(1 ÷ 2) × distance (d) × (distance (d) × gravitational acceleration − 2 × (initial velocity (V) ^ 2) × ((1 ÷ 2) × the sine of (2 × angle of launch (α)))) ÷ ((initial velocity (V) ^ 2) × ((the cosine of (angle of launch (α)), 2)))
Initial vertical velocity (Vy)=-the square root of (2) × the square root of (-gravitational acceleration × (initial height (h) − maximum height (hₘₐₓ)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Initial velocity (V) = 10 m/s, Angle of launch (α) = 10 deg and Gravitational acceleration = 9.8067 m/s². The calculator returns Initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) = 9.848 m/s, Initial vertical velocity (Vy) = 1.736 m/s and Horizontal velocity = 9.848 m/s.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) = 9.848 m/s, Initial vertical velocity (Vy) = 1.736 m/s and Horizontal velocity = 9.848 m/s should be roughly the size you expected from Initial velocity (V) = 10 m/s and Angle of launch (α) = 10 deg.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Speed, opening in meters per second

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Projectile motion calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the angle of launch, the time of flight and the time — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Projectile motion calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ), derived from the angle of launch, the time of flight and the time. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Projectile motion calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the angle of launch, the time of flight and the time, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial velocity (V) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial velocity (V) opens in meters per second and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) = 9.848 m/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Projectile motion calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
